title: The Next Medium: Why Real-Time Interactive Video Changes Everything — Ahmed Ahres, Reactor

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary object is real-time, interactive, infinitely generated video, which is the defining topic of multimodal and realtime systems. Domain selection reflects the demonstrated content (media creation), the stated second model use case (robotics training data), and the reactor platform itself being a substrate other builders integrate against. Stage selection reflects that reactor focuses on serving models for real-time generation, enabling runtime interactivity in sessions, and the closing admission that evaluation remains an open problem. Intermediate fits because the talk is accessible to practitioners but assumes familiarity with model serving, real-time constraints, and the named third-party models. The form is a platform demo with analogy, evidenced by the live cat-into-scene prompt, the gps-to-uber and viewfinder-to-instagram framings, and the explicit integration walkthrough. Evidence is vendor perspective because ahmed is reactor's head of go-to-market presenting his own product, pricing, and roadmap positions.

summary:
Ahmed Ahres opens by introducing himself as Reactor's head of go-to-market and defining world models as real-time interactive video, not Gaussian splatting or extended clips. He uses two historical analogies to argue real time is a qualitative shift: GPS made location continuously queryable, enabling Uber, and the digital viewfinder made filming self-correcting, enabling Instagram and TikTok. Today's batch video models (Veo 3, Sora 2) are framed as slot machines that return immutable files.

He taxonomizes the market into three model classes. Model one is infinite, interactive, real-time video, demonstrated live by injecting a cat into a dog scene mid-generation, unlocking instant-feedback creator control and real-time ad insertion. Model two (e.g., Genie 3) enables character-controllable worlds, with applications beyond games into robotics training data and immersive education, plus Bandersnatch-style interactive movies. Model three, live interactive avatars, he candidly admits is not yet working properly but will impact support, training, sales, gaming, and streaming.

Reactor users are building interactive live streams with voting, medical and cooking simulations, and prompt-driven video editing, the last limited by current model quality. Reactor hosts four third-party models: Helios (ByteDance), Linkbot (Alibaba), LongLive 2 (Nvidia), and Sound Streaming (Nvidia).

In closing, Ahres stresses that real-time infrastructure is fundamentally different from batch. Three challenges dominate: streaming pixels from server to client, maintaining per-session memory so characters remember context when turning left or right, and achieving sub-100ms latency globally by routing users to nearby GPUs rather than centralizing compute. Integration is described as roughly ten lines of code with an API key, with a promo code AIE2026 offering $75 in credits. In Q&A, he explains that higher frame rates are achievable via multi-GPU and quantization, notes that deterministic engines are not built into Reactor but the community open-sources them, and concedes that evaluation of real-time consistency and fidelity remains an unsolved research problem, currently judged by human inspection even at DeepMind.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Opening and definition of world models
sections.summary: Ahmed introduces himself as Reactor's head of go-to-market, shares his CV in computer vision, ML, and iOS/Android games, and argues that world models should be defined as real-time interactive video rather than Gaussian splatting or longer clips, claiming this change will transform content production and consumption.

sections.title: The programmable-video question and speaker background
sections.summary: He contrasts today's passive video with models like Veo 3 and Sora 2 that behave like slot machines, posing the question of what happens when video becomes programmable like software and pixels can be generated in real time.

sections.title: Reactor company background and the batch-video problem
sections.summary: Reactor is introduced as a platform making real-time world models usable, and Ahres reiterates that generated video today is a recording you cannot change, setting up real time as a medium change rather than a speedup.

sections.title: Historical analogies: GPS and the viewfinder
sections.summary: Two analogies argue real time unlocks new categories: GPS made location continuously queryable, enabling Uber, and the digital viewfinder made filming self-correcting, enabling Instagram and TikTok. Programmability lets users address, condition, and change generated video.

sections.title: Model one: infinite, interactive, real-time video
sections.summary: Reactor categorizes the market into three model types, starting with infinite interactive real-time video. A live demo shows a cat being prompted into a dog scene mid-generation. This unlocks creator control via instant feedback and enables real-time advertising keyed to recent viewer behavior, despite brand caution about AI.

sections.title: Model two: controllable character worlds beyond games
sections.summary: Model two, exemplified by Genie 3, allows steering characters and worlds from an image plus text. Beyond games, it enables Bandersnatch-style interactive movies, unlimited robotics training data via simulation, and immersive education by stepping learners into scenarios.

sections.title: Model three: live interactive avatars
sections.summary: Model three covers live interactive avatars for customer support, training, sales, gaming, and streaming. Ahres is candid that avatars are still 'weird' and have not been cracked.

sections.title: What users are building on Reactor
sections.summary: Reactor users are building interactive live streams with voting on X/YouTube/Twitch, medical training simulations exploring drug interventions, cooking simulations, and prompt-driven video editing platforms, the last limited by current model quality.

sections.title: Reactor's hosted model lineup
sections.summary: Reactor hosts four third-party models: Helios (interactive video from ByteDance), Linkbot (world model from Alibaba, like Genie 3), LongLive 2 (Nvidia multi-shot film), and Sound Streaming (Nvidia video-to-video editing for adding effects, removing people, and more).

sections.title: Real-time vs batch infrastructure
sections.summary: Ahres argues that real-time infrastructure cannot reuse batch inference. Three challenges: streaming pixels from server to client adds new complexity, every session is live and must maintain memory (e.g., remembering what happened when a character looked away), and sub-100ms latency requires routing users to nearby GPUs worldwide or the medium breaks.

sections.title: Reactor integration and call to action
sections.summary: Reactor offers roughly ten lines of code integration with an API key and a QR code, plus a promo code AIE2026 giving $75 in credits, framed as a significant amount of compute because the models are made extremely cheap.

sections.title: Q&A: frame rates, IBC, and deterministic engines
sections.summary: Audience questions cover raising the stated 16 FPS to 30 FPS (achievable via multi-GPU and quantization), whether Reactor will present at the International Broadcasting Convention (Ahres was unaware but will look into it), and whether the platform supports deterministic rule-set engines (Reactor does not build them but the developer community open-sources them on top).

sections.title: Q&A: evaluation is an unsolved problem
sections.summary: Asked how algorithm consistency is measured, Ahres concedes this is unsolved across the world-model research community, including DeepMind. Fidelity is easy (pixels), but real-time consistency and quality evaluation currently relies on human visual judgment, with Reactor's research team working on it.

demonstrations: Live demo prompting a cat into a generated dog scene mid-generation to show real-time interactivity.
Reference to Bandersnatch as a prior interactive movie experience that becomes scalable with these models.
Reactor user case studies: interactive live stream with voting, medical simulation, cooking simulation, and prompt-based video editing.
limitations: Avatars remain 'weird' and have not been cracked for customer support or similar use cases.
Video-to-video editing platforms built on these models are limited by current model quality.
Real-time advertising insertion will be slowed by brand caution over AI-generated logos.
Current real-time models struggle with memory: characters can look back and not remember what was happening.
Reactor does not currently build deterministic engines itself, relying on the community to open-source them.
Evaluation of real-time world models for consistency and fidelity is an unsolved research problem, currently relying on human judgment.
quantitativeClaims: Reactor integration is 'maybe 10 lines of code'.
Real-time requires sub-100 millisecond latency anywhere in the world.
Promo code AIE2026 provides $75 worth of credits.
16 FPS was stated as the current frame rate, with 30 FPS achievable via multi-GPU and quantization.
